frequency_question: How often do structural friction points (inter-agency pushback, legal injunctions, statutory procedural requirements, or immediate retaliatory concessions that stall execution) successfully prevent or delay such proposed tariffs before the deadline?
membership_rule: Includes executive-ordered broad sector tariffs or border tax threats announced with short deadlines. Excludes standard multi-year Section 301 or Section 232 investigations with built-in statutory timelines.

cases.name: 2019 Proposed Tariffs on Mexico (Border security threat)

coverage_note: 5 major instances identified where high-level unilateral tariff threats with short windows were deployed; 2 resulted in actual implementation, while 3 were suspended or averted via structural friction/negotiations before the deadline.
known_gaps: Borderline cases involving minor tariff adjustments under routine administrative authorities are excluded.
skeleton: Threats of unilateral tariffs under executive authority within compressed windows (5 cases), noting those that actually materialized without being suspended or withdrawn due to structural/negotiated friction before implementation.
validity_reason: Executive trade enforcement authorities and the mechanisms of trade negotiations remain stable across administrations, though polarization could alter intervention frequencies over a longer horizon.
